title: Introduction to Computability
body:
COMP 2613 asks which problems a computer can solve and how much machine each one requires.
Every other COMP course hands you a problem and asks for a program. This one asks whether a
program can exist.

The course answers that by building a sequence of machines, each strictly stronger than the
one before it. It starts with a machine that remembers nothing beyond which state it is
currently in, adds a stack, then adds an unlimited tape. At every step there is a specific
task the weaker machine provably cannot perform, and constructing that task is the work. The
sequence ends at a machine that models everything any computer can do, and then shows a
problem that machine cannot solve either.

Nothing here is a programming course. The material is proofs, so [[DISCRETE MATH]] is the real
prerequisite. What it produces is used later as [[NP-Complete|NP-completeness]] in
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]], as the [[Finite State Machine|finite state machines]] built
from flip-flops in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], and as the [[Lambda Calculus]] that
[[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] is built on.

## Topics

### Alphabets, strings and languages

Three definitions set up the entire course.

An [[Alphabet]], written $\Sigma$, is a finite non-empty set of symbols. A string is a finite
sequence of symbols from that alphabet, and $\varepsilon$ names the empty string, the one with
no symbols in it. $\Sigma^*$ is the set of every string that can be built from $\Sigma$,
including $\varepsilon$.

A [[Languages|language]] is any set of strings, which is to say any subset of $\Sigma^*$.

```
Σ = {a, b}
Σ* = { ε, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aaa, ... }        infinite
L  = { ab, aabb, aaabbb, ... }  = { aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1 }  a language over Σ
```

That third line is the definition of a problem in this course. Every machine here is a device
that reads a string and answers one question: is this string in the language? A problem such
as "is this number prime" becomes the language of all strings that spell a prime number, so
solving the problem and recognising the language are the same task.

### How things get proved

Proof technique carries as much weight here as content, and two techniques do most of the
work. [[Proof By Induction]] establishes a claim about every string by proving it for
$\varepsilon$ and then proving that adding one symbol preserves it.
[[Proof By Contradiction]] assumes a machine exists, follows the assumption to something
false, and concludes that no such machine exists. Every impossibility result in the course is
the second one, so this is the technique to be fluent in. [[Proof]] covers the general
structure.

### Finite automata

An [[Automata|automaton]] with a fixed number of states has no memory beyond the state it
currently occupies. It reads the input one symbol at a time, moves between states, and accepts
the string if it finishes in an accepting state.

A [[DFA]], a deterministic finite automaton, has exactly one transition leaving each state for
each symbol, so its path through the input is fully determined. Here is one accepting binary
strings that end in `01`, where $q_0$ is the start state and $q_2$ is accepting:

```
state | on 0 | on 1 | accepting
------+------+------+----------
 q0   |  q1  |  q0  |    no       nothing useful seen yet
 q1   |  q1  |  q2  |    no       just saw a 0
 q2   |  q1  |  q0  |    yes      just saw 01
```

Trace `1101`: q0 →1→ q0 →1→ q0 →0→ q1 →1→ q2, which is accepting. Trace `100`: q0 →1→ q0
→0→ q1 →0→ q1, which is rejecting. The three states are the machine's entire memory, and each
one means something: nothing pending, a zero pending, a complete `01` just seen.

An [[NFA]], a nondeterministic finite automaton, relaxes that. A state may have several
transitions on one symbol, none at all, or $\varepsilon$-moves that consume no input. It
accepts a string when at least one path through it ends in an accepting state.
[[Nondeterminism]] makes machines far easier to design, and it adds no recognising power at
this level. The subset construction converts any NFA into a DFA by making each DFA state a set
of NFA states, which costs up to $2^n$ states for an $n$-state NFA and always terminates.

[[Regular Expressions]] describe exactly the same class of languages these machines recognise,
which is the [[Regular Languages]]. Three notations, one class. That class is closed under
union, concatenation, star, intersection and complement, so any language built from regular
languages using those operations is regular, and complement is proved by swapping the
accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA.

### The pumping lemma

Showing a language is regular means exhibiting a machine. Showing a language is not regular
needs an argument covering every possible machine, and the [[Pumping Lemma]] is that argument
packaged for reuse.

The reasoning: a DFA has some finite number of states $p$. Any accepted string longer than $p$
must revisit a state, because there are more steps than states. The section of the string
consumed between those two visits forms a loop, and a loop can be taken any number of times,
so repeating that section produces another string the machine also accepts.

Formally, if $L$ is regular there exists $p$ such that every string $s \in L$ with
$|s| \geq p$ splits as $s = xyz$ with $|y| > 0$, $|xy| \leq p$, and $xy^iz \in L$ for every
$i \geq 0$.

Applied to $\{a^n b^n\}$, the language of some number of `a`s followed by the same number of
`b`s:

```
take s = aᵖbᵖ, which is in L and long enough
|xy| ≤ p forces x and y to sit inside the a's, so y = aᵏ for some k > 0
pump i = 2:  xy²z = a^(p+k) b^p
p + k ≠ p, so the string has more a's than b's and is outside L
```

The lemma promised that string stays in $L$ and it does not, so $L$ is not regular. Every use
of the lemma is a [[Proof By Contradiction]] of that shape, and the underlying reason is
concrete: matching the counts requires remembering a number without bound, and a finite
automaton has a fixed number of states to remember it with.

### Grammars and pushdown automata

A stack is exactly enough memory to count. [[Pushdown Automata]] are finite automata with a
stack attached, pushing on the way in and popping on the way out, which handles $\{a^n b^n\}$
by pushing a marker per `a` and popping one per `b`.

[[Context-Free Grammars]] generate the same class from the other direction. A grammar is a set
of rules that rewrite a symbol into a string of symbols, starting from one start symbol:

```
S → aSb | ε

S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaaSbbb ⇒ aaabbb        generates aⁿbⁿ
```

Every language a context-free grammar generates is one a pushdown automaton recognises, and
the reverse holds too. This class covers matched brackets, nested structure and the syntax of
essentially every programming language, which is why a parser has a stack inside it.
$\{a^n b^n c^n\}$ sits outside the class, because one stack can match one pair of counts and
loses the information while doing it. Nondeterminism does matter at this level: a
nondeterministic pushdown automaton recognises strictly more languages than a deterministic
one, which differs from the finite automaton case.

The [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] is the ladder itself:

| Class | Machine | Memory | Example language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regular | finite automaton | states only | strings ending in `01` |
| Context-free | pushdown automaton | one stack | $a^n b^n$, matched brackets |
| Context-sensitive | linear bounded automaton | tape bounded by input length | $a^n b^n c^n$ |
| Recursively enumerable | [[Turing Machine]] | unbounded tape | anything computable |

Each row adds memory to the row below it, and each containment is strict, proved by exhibiting
a language in the higher class and absent from the lower one.

### Turing machines and undecidability

A [[Turing Machine]] is a finite control attached to an unbounded tape it can read, write and
move along in both directions. That is the whole model, and it computes everything any
computer can compute. The Church-Turing thesis is the claim that anything effectively
computable is computable by one, and the evidence for it is convergence: the
[[Lambda Calculus]] has no tape, no states and no memory, and it computes exactly the same
class of functions.

Two words separate the last two rows of the hierarchy. A language is decidable when some
machine always halts and answers correctly. A language is recognisable when some machine halts
and accepts every string in the language, while possibly running forever on strings outside
it. Recognisable is the weaker property, and the gap between the two is where
[[Undecidability]] lives.

The halting problem asks whether a given program halts on a given input. No program decides it,
and the argument is short. Suppose `halts(P, x)` exists and returns true exactly when program
`P` halts on input `x`. Build:

```python
def trouble(P):
    if halts(P, P):
        while True: pass    # loop forever
    else:
        return              # halt
```

Now ask what `trouble(trouble)` does. If it halts, then `halts(trouble, trouble)` was true, so
the branch taken was the infinite loop and it did not halt. If it fails to halt, then
`halts(trouble, trouble)` was false, so it took the returning branch and halted. Both answers
contradict themselves, so `halts` cannot exist. That is diagonalisation, and
[[Godel's Theorem]] is the same self-reference producing a true statement no formal system of
arithmetic can prove.

### Complexity

[[NP-Complete]] takes the last step, from problems no algorithm solves to problems whose only
algorithms are too slow to run. P is the class solvable in polynomial time. NP is the class
where a proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time, which is a much weaker
requirement: finding a [[Hamiltonian Cycle]] in a graph is hard, and checking a proposed one
takes a single pass along the route.

A problem is NP-complete when it lies in NP and every problem in NP reduces to it, meaning any
NP problem can be rewritten as an instance of it in polynomial time. An efficient algorithm
for one NP-complete problem would therefore give an efficient algorithm for all of them. SAT
was the first problem proved NP-complete, by Cook and Levin. Proving a new problem NP-complete
means reducing a known NP-complete problem to it, and the direction of that reduction is the
thing to get right: the known-hard problem becomes an instance of the new one. Whether P
equals NP is open. [[Time Complexity]] and [[Algorithm]] supply the measurement machinery.

### Other models

[[Cellular Automata]] reach Turing completeness from a grid of cells updating by local rules,
with Conway's Game of Life as the standard example, which demonstrates that the ceiling is
reached by extremely simple systems. [[Simulation]] covers one machine imitating another,
which is the technique behind every equivalence result in the course, including the subset
construction and the Church-Turing evidence.

## Related courses

- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) is the prerequisite, supplying [[Proof]], [[Sets]],
  [[Induction]], [[Proof By Contradiction]] and [[Direct Proof]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) is where [[NP-Complete]] first appears in practice
  as the [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], and where [[Stack]] and [[Graph]] exist as implementations.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] carries P against NP and [[Time Complexity]] further.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) builds [[Finite State Machine|finite state machines]]
  as circuits, where the state is stored in flip-flops.
- [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]] (COMP 3649) starts from [[Lambda Calculus]] and turns
  [[Nondeterminism]] into a programming technique.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) contains the [[Dangling else]], which is
  an ambiguous grammar in the vocabulary of this course.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] covers [[Turing Machine]], [[Chomsky Hierarchy]],
  [[Regular Languages]], [[Godel's Theorem]] and [[Cellular Automata]] in its own chapters.
- [[SYMBOLIC LOGIC]] (PHIL 1179) builds the formal systems this course reasons about, and
  ends where this one starts: its [[Metatheory]] section states soundness and completeness
  for first-order logic, and [[Godel's Theorem]] is what happens to completeness once the
  system can describe arithmetic.
